blocks.x: We might start at the very beginning though and ask Mr. Bertrand, how do you pronounce the name?
B-E-R-T-R-A-N-D, Bertrando Profondo.
And your name is James?
James, Jimmy Bertrand.
Everybody calls you Jimmy.
Yes, sir.
Where were you born? I was born in Deluxe, Mississippi, 1900. Can you give us the exact date? Yes, Tuesday. Oh, you know the day even. I mean, what was my...
Tuesday, and my uncle was Alphonse Fuzan, F-A-R-Z-A-N, Alphonse. He's the first man left out of Biloxi with the first Creole band. Now, that's the old Creole band, the first one with Freddie Kepard.
Oh, what did he play?
Bass fiddle.
Oh, he was the bass. Three string, you know?
You got it there.
Yeah, you got that three string, the old thing.
See, that's Alphonse Fuzan.
That's my... How's his name spelled?
F-A-R-Z-A-N. That's Creole. Yes. Uh-huh. I'm saying. That's Alphonse.
And what was your exact birthday? When was your birthday? February... Oh, not it.
February the 24th, 1900. 1900. That makes me right on time.
Yeah, it's like Louis Armstrong born the same year. It's on the 4th of July. I mean, let's say.
It's the same.
Did you start in music down there? No.
I started music at the... When I came to Chicago in 1913. I went to the Catholic Church. I'm a Catholic.
Oh, yeah.

And Father Kelly was my pastor with the Reagan Colts over at 59th and Halstead. You know, not 59th and Halstead. I mean it's 55th and Halstead. And I started taking lessons from Erskine Tate's father. That's old man Jackson at 31st.
That's the long run.

Yeah, that's right. And at that particular time you had... We were all taking lessons. All the boys were down there. And we took lessons. What I mean by taking lessons... The E-Light No. 1 was down there.
Was that where Tony Jackson played? Tony Jackson!
Yeah!
You got it?

Me and Tony used to go... You know when he wrote the song there? Yeah, pretty big. Me and Tony. And what's the other fellow's name? Let me get it right now. Not only Tony. What you call him? But he wrote all those songs. Tony died.
Yes, I knew you.
Well anyway, we all started around 35th. Right on that corner. See, I worked a long time right on that corner. What do you call it? State and 35th?
Oh, yes.
The States Theater? Yes. When I was a kid I played music there and went to school around there and all them boys
just like anybody you could name. You have to question me because it's not true. Who had the band there? Who was the leader? The band in the- At the States Theater. The State?
Bailey.
Bailey.
Yeah. From Paris, Texas. Piano player. He's out in LA now. He's out there with the man. What's his name? Oh, I can't remember.
Kid Ori. He's out there with Ori, yeah.
Yeah. They're out there together, yeah.
I was going to ask, when you started on the drums, is that your first instrument or? Mm-hmm. On the drums? Mm-hmm. Yeah. And what was the first band you played with? So many bands. I guess so many.
The best band I've played was Erskine Tate.
Is that at the Van Dome?
I played with Ty, that's the Van Dome for years. We had the best band anybody at all.
But I heard, yeah.
I took lessons from the best musicians in this country. You know what I mean? I know.
People told me you were a really finished drummer.

I mean you knew all of the instruments. Me and Mr. Cusick, me and Mr. Roy Knapp, if you say that, let Mr. Roy Knapp say something about it. He was the man from the, what do you call it, the Minneapolis Symphony.
Oh yes, I've heard of him. And Roy's downtown now, he's taking care of everybody. He has a drum book out, I think.
And he, that's Roy, that's my buddy. And another fellow, let me get them together now, uh, got dog my tootin' time, Art Layfield. Oh yes. Used to be with Paul Ash. Mm-hmm.

That was my tutor too. You remember Paul Ash? Yes, I used to hear him at the theater down there. Oriental was one of those theaters. Well he was at the Oriental and the McVickers. The McVickers, that's where I had him. Yeah. I used to take Lesman Wren. Then I got bigger than him.
I was at the Chicago Fair there. Mm-hmm. I was lookin' down at him. I'm with Eddie South's band now, see. You remember Eddie South? Yeah.
Oh sure, I know him. I mean, it's drama. It goes all over the world with Eddie. Did you go to Europe?

segments.title: Opening: pronouncing and spelling Bertrand's name
segments.summary: The interviewer asks how to pronounce the name; Bertrand spells it and confirms he is James, called Jimmy.

segments.title: Birth in Mississippi and uncle Alphonse Farzan
segments.summary: Bertrand was born in Deluxe, Mississippi, on February 24, 1900. His uncle Alphonse Farzan played bass in the first Creole band out of Biloxi with Freddie Keppard.

segments.title: Coming to Chicago and first music lessons
segments.summary: He began music in Chicago in 1913 through the Catholic church and took lessons from Erskine Tate's father, with the other boys.

segments.title: State and 35th: Tony Jackson and the States Theater band
segments.summary: He recalls Tony Jackson and the 35th and State corner where he worked as a kid, and the States Theater leader Bailey, a pianist from Paris, Texas, now in Los Angeles with Kid Ory.

segments.title: Drums and playing with Erskine Tate at the Vendome
segments.summary: Asked about his first instrument and band, Bertrand says drums and names Erskine Tate's band at the Vendome as the best he played in for years.

segments.title: Drum teachers: Roy Knapp, Art Layfield and Paul Ash
segments.summary: Bertrand lists his teachers, including Roy Knapp and Art Layfield, formerly with Paul Ash. The interviewer says Layfield taught him too and they discuss the Oriental and McVickers theaters.

segments.title: With Eddie South's band and a question about Europe
segments.summary: Bertrand mentions working with Eddie South's band, and the interviewer asks whether he went to Europe.
